source.title: On the Universality of the Double Descent Peak in Ridgeless Regression

record.tranche_reason: The paper analytically studies interpolation-related generalization error in ridgeless regression using non-asymptotic bounds and exact distribution-specific results, rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own theoretical bounds and experiments on noise-induced error (ENoise). Results cited from other papers, including their double-descent findings, are not recorded as rows. ENoise is a component of expected excess risk and a lower bound on it, not the full test error. Experimental curves appear only as figures; the text describes their setups but does not give curve values or a textual account of their shapes.
record.test_reason: The paper proves a distribution-independent lower bound and exact formulas for label-noise-induced error (ENoise) in ridgeless regression with general feature maps. This bears on whether a noise-driven interpolation peak and second descent hold outside deep networks. It uses theory plus random-feature simulations, not the original deep-network sweeps. ENoise lower-bounds expected excess risk and equals it when the target function is zero.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors prove that, with label noise, ridgeless regression performs poorly around the interpolation threshold for any feature map satisfying their assumptions. This covers random deep NNs with analytic activations, random Fourier features and polynomial kernels. The bound is asymptotically sharp and quite sharp far from the threshold, but underestimates the peak height. Avoiding the peak essentially requires violating full rank (FRK) or moving far from p≈n.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops non-asymptotic theoretical lower bounds and exact formulas for ridgeless regression, with accompanying random-feature experiments, rather than reproducing the original deep-network training sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different ENoise outcomes across feature distributions, feature-map families, activation functions, whitening, and model dimensions. It notes that ReLU, ELU and SELU networks do not satisfy FRK; it also notes high estimation variance near n ∈ {28, …, 32} in Figure 1 and unstable, heavy-tailed estimates for ReLU in the underparameterized regime.

fits_no_version.finding: Whitening features never increases and often reduces ENoise in the overparameterized regime; it makes no difference when p≤n (Remark G.1, Fig. C.2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature covariance shape affects noise-induced error only past the interpolation threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: NN feature maps trained to minimize ENoise did not beat the uniform-sphere distribution, which is conjectured optimal (Fig. 1, Remark G.3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The noise-induced interpolation peak cannot be engineered away by feature design while preserving the ability to interpolate.

record.problems: The broad theorem is a lower bound on the label-noise contribution, not a characterization of total risk. Several empirical results are available only as plots, and the paper reports high estimation variance near interpolation in some experiments, including heavy-tailed ReLU estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were left out. C.2 and C.6 are whitened or relative presentations of results already represented by the feature-sweep figures; cited results from other studies were excluded.

untested.parts: No trained deep networks. Only random-feature or kernel models with a linear readout.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
Multiple/triple peaks, varying noise levels, and removal of the peak by optimally tuned regularization are not tested.
No re-expression in terms of an effective parameter count.

missing.what: Optimized NN feature maps (n=15, n=60) still show ENoise at or above the sphere and lower bound near the threshold. This supports universality of the peak.
Counterexample: uniform distribution on basis vectors (histogram regression) violates FRK and has ENoise below the lower bound over a large range of n.
missing.locator: Appendix D, Example D.1, Figure D.1, Remark D.2

missing.what: The lower bound is asymptotically sharp, giving σ²/(γ−1) as p/n→γ. The paper says it is quite sharp for p≫n and p≪n but underestimates the peak height.
Achieving ENoise<εσ² requires p<εn or p>n/ε unless FRK is violated.

record.verdict_notes: T2: theoretical/analytic study of the double-descent peak outside deep networks. ENoise is a lower bound on expected excess risk and equals it for a zero target, so it is a valid but partial measure of test error. The reader's limits_scope labels based only on the choice of measure were dropped, because they are not conditions where the effect fails. The Gaussian formulas (Theorem 12) were previously derived by Belkin et al. 2020 and Breiman & Freedman; the paper re-proves them. Figure-only appendix curves cannot be read from the text.

versions.untested_parts: The p-sweep in random neural-network feature maps measures ENoise, not full test error in deep networks; the figure-only curve does not establish the claimed shape.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
The theoretical and experimental results concern ENoise, not the full test error; the sample-wise experiments do not provide textual curve values.
Exact distribution-specific results are for ridgeless linear regression and ENoise; the general lower bound is not an exact full-risk curve.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations across axes.

The paper analyzes a label-noise contribution and reports noise-conditioned results. It does not test multiple or triple peaks, varying label-noise levels, or whether optimal regularization removes the peak.
No re-expression of the curve in terms of an effective parameter count.

relationships.reason: ENoise rises with n for n<p−1 and is infinite near n≈p (r3–r5, r7, r8).
relationships.display_finding: The expected noise contribution rose with n for n < p − 1 and became infinite near n ≈ p.

statements.correction: Appendix D: a non-FRK orthonormal-basis distribution violates the proposed bound; equally probable histogram bins realize this distribution. Section 5: activations with linear regions can violate FRK. These findings restrict the theorem's applicability; they do not show a noise-independent peak or failure of optimally tuned regularization.
statements.problem: The reported assumptions and counterexample are accurate, but failure of this lower bound does not establish a limitation of V6's noise-dependence claim.
